back: Finding a password by trial and error, trying common passwords and then every combination.
Capturing data as it travels across a network, e.g. with a packet sniffer or by eavesdropping on Wi-Fi.
A botnet floods a server with requests so genuine users cannot access the service.
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, usually by exploiting a security weakness.
Phishing: user clicks a link in a fake message. Pharming: malicious code or a corrupted DNS server redirects the user even when the correct address is typed.
Manipulating people (trust, fear, curiosity) into giving away information or access, e.g. fake IT calls, baiting, shoulder surfing.
Disguising an email, caller ID or IP address so it appears to come from a trusted source.
10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10 000, which is why devices limit wrong attempts.

front: Effects of cyber attacks on organisations?
back: Financial loss, lost reputation and trust, downtime, repair costs and legal penalties for failing to protect data.
